name: Nikhil Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a firm that defends insurance companies. When someone claims after a car crash or a fall in a supermarket, the insurer sends us the file and we work out whether to fight it or settle. A normal day is reading medical reports, writing to the other side, and drafting advice to the insurer on what the claim's worth. I've got about sixty files open at any time, which sounds like a lot until you meet the people with a hundred and twenty.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Steady, but I'm not a star. I'm careful, sometimes too careful, and the partner I work for, Mrs Haines, says I take too long to make a call on value. I use the firm's AI tool now and then to summarise medical records, when I'm behind. Outside work, I got married last year, and my wife teaches at a primary school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that most of the fuss was sales talk. People still crash cars and still need a lawyer to argue about it. I'd say that to my dad and my friends, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and I can get on with getting better. I've got about nine months saved and a small share in my dad's plumbing supplies business. Nothing in this picture threatens that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get quicker at making calls on value. I'd use the summary tool a bit more, since it works. And Priya and I would start saving for a bigger place, maybe with a garden, for when kids come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the normal world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the tool when you're behind. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit more each year. It's good at pulling the key dates out of a medical record. I still read the doctor's conclusion myself, because that's where cases are won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualify properly, get to mid-level, and start a family with Priya in two or three years. Maybe move closer to my parents. Ordinary things.

do: Work on making **faster calls** on what a claim is worth.
Use the **summary tool** a bit more on medical records.
Save with my wife Priya for a **bigger place** with a garden.

fieldNote: He's **secure** in money and family support, so the plateau feels normal.

steps.text: Keep handling about sixty insurance claim files
Use the summary tool on every long medical record
Save with Priya for a bigger house with a garden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and firms have to keep up. That's what Mrs Haines would say too. To friends I'd say I'm watching it closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Insurers would settle the small claims with software and only send our firm the big or tricky ones. That's fewer files, which means fewer juniors, and I'm a slow junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tool on every file, not just when I'm behind, and ask to go on the firm's training. I'd push to get onto the bigger, contested claims that go to court. And Priya and I would wait a year on the bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not hopeless. I'd have time and options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Insurers already use a lot of software. What would change for your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer, bigger files. The insurers' own systems would handle anything simple, like whiplash claims with a standard value. Firms like mine would cut the junior intake and keep the ones who can run a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about your dad's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My dad's always said there's a place for me if law doesn't work out, and I've always said no thanks. In this picture I'd start learning the business on Saturdays, just to know it.

fieldNote: He sees his **file count** dropping and himself among the juniors at risk.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tool on every claim file

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and it's going to hurt ordinary families. I'd say we need to stick together, families and communities, rather than wait for the government. To my dad I'd say I might need that place after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job as it is ends. If the AI can value a claim better than my boss, the insurers won't pay our firm to do it. I'd still have money and family, so I wouldn't be lost, but I'd be starting again at twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join my dad's business within the first year, learning the ordering and the customers. I'd keep the savings as they are and pause the house. I'd ask Priya if we should still try for a baby next year, and I think we would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's frightening, but I know where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your wife see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would be steady. Her job's mostly with children in a room, so it would last longer than mine. She'd say we'd be fine, and she'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family business really be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. Plumbers still need pipes, and robots for hands-on work come about three years later. But the ordering and invoicing side would change straight away, so I'd be the one who sets up the AI for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and people should use it. I'd tell friends and family to plan. At work I'd keep my head down and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me do both. I'd stay in law for a few more years, earn well, and learn the family business on the side. When AGI arrives I'd move across with savings and some knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools daily, push for bigger files, and spend Saturdays at my dad's business. Priya and I would buy the bigger place in year two, since I'd still be earning. I'd put a bit more into savings each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. It's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn, save, learn, then make the move before I'm pushed. Get two or three years of good pay and experience first. Five years is long enough to do it in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really anyone. The companies are competing, which is how markets work. I'd just want the government to stay out of the way and let families and businesses adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for sensible people. To friends I'd say get on with life. At work I'd keep learning the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to have a decent law career first, maybe make senior associate. The thinking side of the job goes in 2036, but I'd see it coming and could move to the family business before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in law and use the tools more each year. Priya and I would buy the house and have kids on our normal timeline. I'd keep a foot in the family business, a few Saturdays a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. It doesn't change my life yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, would you still be in law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably until about 2033, then into the business. Maybe as the person who handles its contracts and suppliers. A law degree's never wasted in a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something you can do with your hands as well as your head. Look after your family, because family is what holds when jobs don't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pushed rather than choosing. What would help is time, and for my family business to be strong enough to take me. I don't need the government, I need my family and a bit of warning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lucky I am. Lots of juniors don't have a dad with a business. I'd be fine, but some of the people I trained with would not.

headlineQuote: I don't need the government, I need my family and a bit of warning.
portrait: A **junior solicitor** defending insurers against injury claims, with about sixty files open.
He's **careful but slow** to call a claim's value, and uses AI now and then.
**Nine months** saved, a teacher wife and his dad's plumbing supplies business back him up.
He's **anxious** with steady change or AGI in two years, and uneasy with longer warning.
His plan is to move into the **family business** on his own terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be pushed out rather than choosing to leave.
whatWouldHelp: **Time** to prepare and a **family business** strong enough to take him.
